tip: 'Hacerse' in impersonal expressions: 'se me hace tarde' = it's getting late for me. The indirect object pronoun shows who is affected.
Why the -s on 'cumpleaños'? It's cumple + años – 'completes years'. One birthday, always spelled plural: hoy es mi cumpleaños.
'Escribo' covers both 'I write' and 'I'm writing'. Spanish rarely needs an -ing form – the simple present does double duty.
Weather uses "hacer" in Spanish: hace calor (it's hot), hace frío (it's cold), hace sol (it's sunny), hace viento (it's windy).
"Para llevar" = for taking away. Standard phrase for takeout food.
Very sunny? Spanish says much SUN: 'hace mucho sol'. Sol is a noun, so muy is impossible – muy pairs with adjectives, mucho with nouns.
No -ly needed: 'rápido' works as its own adverb. 'Como demasiado rápido' – many everyday adjectives moonlight as adverbs unchanged.
Order water abroad and you'll be asked: ¿con o sin gas? 'Sin gas' = still, con gas = sparkling – literally without/with gas.
Estar for current condition: "¿Cómo estás?" How someone IS right now (condition, mood, health) → estar.
'Ilusión' is not an illusion here – it's happy anticipation. 'Me hace ilusión verte' = I'm thrilled to see you. A famously positive false friend.
Es ingeniero – no 'un'. After ser, a profession works like a label, so Spanish drops the article. It returns only with an adjective: es un ingeniero brillante.
"Para" = by/for (deadline): "Necesito esto para el lunes." Para sets the time limit.
"Al" is a contraction of "a" + "el" (to the). Spanish has two mandatory contractions: al (a + el) and del (de + el).
Grande after the noun means big in size: familia grande. Slide it in front and it shrinks to gran – una gran familia – and the meaning shifts to 'great'.
You don't 'be' right in Spanish – you have it: tienes razón is literally 'you have reason'. Same trick as tener hambre (hunger) and tener sueño (sleepiness).
Para here aims at a destination: vamos para el aeropuerto = heading toward it. Swap in por and you'd be passing by way of the airport – route, not goal.
Estar for appearance now: "Estás muy guapa hoy." How someone looks right now (vs. ser for general beauty).
puede could mean "he/she can" or "you (formal) can". puedes is unambiguous – always informal you. Spanish reuses 3rd-person for formal.

english: I want to rent a car.
tip: 'Carro' = car in Latin America; in Spain a carro is a cart – they say coche. Same rental, different word depending where you land.
Tener + noun for physical states: tener sed (be thirsty), tener hambre (be hungry).
'Que + subjunctive' expresses wishes: 'que descanses' = may you rest / rest well. The subjunctive conveys hope or desire.
'De ... a ...' expresses ranges: 'de lunes a viernes' = from Monday to Friday. Days of the week are lowercase in Spanish.
English stacks nouns: plug adapter. Spanish reverses with de: 'adaptador de enchufes' – adapter OF plugs. Main noun first, always.
Ve is the irregular command of ir; add te (from irse, to take yourself off) and you get vete – a brisk 'off you go.'
'En casa', no article, means at home in the abstract sense. En la casa points at the physical building – with the article it's the place, without it it's the concept.
No 'does' needed: Spanish negates with a bare no before the verb. 'No tiene wifi' = it doesn't have wifi. One little word does it all.
'Ella' is optional here – 'quiere' already shows who. Native speakers drop subject pronouns unless contrasting (I, not him).
Desde hace años is literally 'since it makes years'. Spanish counts elapsed time with hace, so plain present conozco does the job of English's 'I have known'.
Es bueno rates the coffee's overall quality. Está bueno would praise this particular cup – tasty right now. Ser gives the general judgment; estar describes the current instance.
Sun and heat use hace, but rain and snow are full verbs: 'está nevando' = it's snowing (nevar). Nieva, llueve – no hace in sight.
